proposals.impact: prevent content gap; single queued post is one failure away from a dry feed
proposals.observation: The three most recent published posts all address a fear of failing or being found out around money ("scared I'll fail," "everyone has it figured out except me," "hoping THIS one finally fixes everything"). The Money Avoidance automation is the highest-volume sender and has a 52.63% open rate, which means a meaningful share of the active audience identifies with avoidance patterns. The pattern that sits underneath avoidance and course-buying is the reflexive tab-close: someone opens their banking app, sees a number, and closes it before the feeling fully registers. That specific moment has not appeared in the recent post titles and it maps directly to the £150k gym-bag story — the awareness of a number that exists but is not being looked at.
proposals.proposal: Write a short blog post (600-800 words) that opens on the tab-close moment rather than the emotion. The gym-bag story or the unopened tax-return tab can anchor the middle. The post should not promise a fix; it should name the moment with enough precision that someone who does this every morning feels, for the first time, that someone has noticed. This serves double duty: it refills the queue and it is the kind of post that converts Avoidance subscribers who are opening emails but not yet clicking through.
proposals.new_text:
---
title: "Why do I check my balance then close the tab before the number loads?"
pubDate: "2026-09-11"
description: "The tab-close is not laziness. It is the body's fastest available exit from a feeling it has learned to treat as dangerous."
tags: ["money avoidance", "behavioural finance", "quiet awareness"]
---

There is a specific half-second between opening your banking app and the balance appearing on screen.

Most people who do what you do — earn a reasonable salary, mean to sort this out, own three unread finance books — close the app in that half-second. Not after seeing a bad number. Before seeing any number at all.

Joel noticed this in himself when he had roughly £150,000 sitting in a current account earning nothing. The money was there. The number existed. He had a gym bag full of gym kit he hadn't used in four months on the same floor as his laptop. Both things were present. Neither was being looked at.

That is not a discipline problem. It is not a knowledge gap. It is a very efficient system your brain built to keep you from feeling something it once decided was intolerable.

The feeling usually formed a long time before you had any money to look at. A parent's voice when a bill arrived. A conversation that stopped when you walked into the room. A number that, once seen, could not be unseen and changed something permanently. The brain filed that under "opening this door = pain" and has been enforcing the rule ever since.

So you tab away. You swipe the notification off. You tell yourself you'll look properly on Sunday. Sunday becomes the Sunday after. The money sits or the debt grows or the tax return tab stays minimised in the browser you use for everything else, so you see it every day without ever quite seeing it.

The honest question is not "why can't I get organised?" The honest question is: what does the number represent, in the story you have been carrying about yourself and money?

For some people it represents proof of a fear they have never said aloud. For others it is evidence that they have not yet become the person they were supposed to become. For others still it is the one thing they cannot control in a life where they control nearly everything else, and not looking means it cannot confirm the worst.

None of these are character flaws. All of them are learnable patterns, which means they can be examined.

The starting point is not a budget spreadsheet. It is a quieter thing: sitting with the tab open for ten seconds without closing it, noticing what arrives in the chest or the jaw or the top of the shoulders, and asking that sensation what it is trying to protect.

That is the work underneath the organising. That is what changes the pattern rather than managing it.

Joel Burgess, MSc Behavioural Economics | Qualified Financial Planner
